mule deer.summary: Montana's mule deer peaked around 2017 and then dropped by about a third, with the southeast (Region 7) hit hardest by drought, hard winters and disease. Eastern herds have been climbing back since 2024 thanks to mild winters and good fawn crops, but several southwest and south-central trend areas are still well below average.

findings.text: FWP's modeled statewide mule deer estimate peaked at 386,175 in 2017 and fell to 255,989 in 2023, 17% below the 10-year average of 306,738 (FWP says pre-2015 estimates are not comparable).
Region 7 (southeast) fell from about 135,000 deer in 2016 to 55,604 in 2023, 41% below average; 2022 spring counts alone were 36% below 2021 and 47% below the long-term average.
FWP blamed the 2020-2023 drought, hard winters, low fawn recruitment and EHD/bluetongue outbreaks that recur every 7-10 years; Region 7 B licenses were cut from 11,000 (2020) to 1,000 (2023-2025).
In June 2023 the Commission made 15 districts buck-only for mule deer: HD 301 (R3), HDs 410-471 (R4), HDs 621-622 (R6) and HDs 700-705 (R7).
Recovery started in 2024: Region 7 was up 20% in 2024 and reached 17% below average by 2026 with 55 fawns per 100 adults; Region 6 density rose 32% in 2026 to slightly above average.
Region 6 still cut antlerless B licenses from 6,200 (2023) to 2,825 (2024) to 1,425 (2025); HDs 600/640/670 carried 8-14% CWD prevalence over three years and 18-28% in adult bucks.

After two mild winters, 2026 southwest Montana fawn ratios were strong (Bridger Range 53 per 100 adults, 66% above average), but the Big Timber trend areas (HDs 525/580) were 53-60% below average and Brackett Creek near Livingston 40% below.
Bitterroot research (HDs 204/270, 2015-2018) found adult doe survival of 0.80 a year and 91-95% pregnancy, so doe die-offs did not explain that herd's decline.

whitetail.summary: FWP doesn't count whitetails directly. It tracks them through harvest and spring fawn surveys, and those show a species that rebounds fast but gets knocked back by disease (EHD) in the river bottoms of eastern Montana and by hard winters in the northwest. The 2021 and 2025 EHD outbreaks led to license cuts, while western harvest stayed strong.

findings.text: FWP uses about 36 fawns per 100 adults in spring as the line for a stable or growing whitetail population in western Montana.

Swan Valley (HD 130) recruitment fell from 53 fawns per 100 adults in 2016 to 25 in 2018 after two severe winters, and FWP made the district buck-only in 2019; HD 130's 2022 buck harvest (393) was under 40% of its 1995-2022 average.
After the hard 2022-23 winter, Region 1 spring recruitment ranged from 17 (HD 120) to 45 (HD 123); it recovered to 34-54 in 2024 and 39 to nearly 70 in 2025.
EHD killed nearly 400 whitetails west of Missoula in 2013, the first documented outbreak west of the Continental Divide in Montana.

The 2021 EHD outbreak along the Milk, Missouri and lower Yellowstone rivers led FWP to cut Region 6 surplus B licenses by 2,000; by 2023 Region 6 trend-area density was 6.2 deer per sq mi, 40% below the 10.4 average.

In 2025 suspected EHD/bluetongue hit Eureka, Plains, Missoula and NE Montana; the Commission capped Region 6 B licenses at 2,000, and spring 2026 recruitment near Missoula dropped to 17.9 (HD 201) and 15.2 (HD 202) from about 77-78 a year earlier.
Statewide whitetail harvest was 45,369 in 2022 and 40,579 in 2025; Region 2's 2025 buck harvest (5,103) beat its 2004-2025 average of 4,692.

elk.summary: Elk are doing well overall: FWP counted about 143,000 in its 2023 report, up from about 135,000 in 2019, and most regions sit within the new 2023 management plan's goal ranges. Valley and foothill units with lots of private land are over their goals, while backcountry units like the Bob Marshall and the Missouri River Breaks are well under them.

findings.text: FWP's statewide minimum count rose from 134,557 (2019) to 143,310 in the 2023 report (3-5-yr average 140,679), within the 2023-plan goal range of 96,015-151,425; under the old 2005 plan the state was far over its 92,138 objective.
In 2023, Regions 2-6 were 'At' their goal ranges while Region 1 (2,146 elk in countable districts) and Region 7 (5,100) were 'Below'.

Units well over goal include Devil's Kitchen 445/455 (5,989 vs 2,500-3,500), Crazy Mountains 580 (5,141 vs 2,500-4,000), HD 213 (2,424 vs 920-1,380) and Northern Yellowstone 313 (5,142 vs 3,000-5,000); HD 360 hit a record 6,207 in 2022.
In the Bob Marshall, HD 140 dropped from 344 elk counted (2004) to 67 (2023), with calf ratios as low as 3 per 100 cows (2009); FWP's Region 1 goal is at least 25 calves per 100 cows.
In the southern Bitterroot (2011-2014), elk calf survival was 0.55 in summer and 0.73 in winter; mountain lions were the leading known cause of death and better summer forage raised survival.
Collared Sapphire Mountains cows spent far less time on public land than bulls, and only 1 of 39 cows was harvested, which helps explain over-objective herds on private land.
After drought and the long 2022-23 winter, Missouri River Breaks elk (HDs 620-630) were 56% below their long-term average and 41% below objective in 2024; antlerless licenses were cut 69%.
Early deep snow in fall 2022 pushed Yellowstone-area elk to winter range during rifle season, and harvest ran 150-250% above average.

antelope.summary: Pronghorn are the species most vulnerable to winter. They crashed after the 2010-11 winter in northeast Montana, then rebuilt to roughly 155,000-159,000 statewide by 2022-2025, with southeast Montana counts in 2025 the best since 2008. Southwest Montana (Region 3) is the exception: drought and the brutal 2022-23 winter left many districts at record lows and led FWP to cut tags sharply.

findings.text: Winter 2010-11 brought about nine feet of snow near Glasgow; about 1,000 pronghorn were killed by trains, at least 200 died at a single haystack, and 2,500-3,000 were stranded along Fort Peck Reservoir. HDs 630 and 670 had the worst declines.
By 2013 Region 7 pronghorn were still 50% below their long-term average and 66% below the 2006 peak; bluetongue had 'decimated much of the herd' in Region 5 in 2008.
Statewide totals rebuilt from 138,288 (2015) to 155,279 (2022) and about 159,000 (2025); Region 7's 2025 aerial counts were the highest since 2008 and 41% above the 10-year average.
Back-to-back hard winters in 2017-19 dropped HD 512 to 264 pronghorn in 2018, the lowest since 1981, with just 23 fawns per 100 does vs a 59 average; either-sex licenses were cut from 75 to 50.
Winter 2022-23 killed more than 30% of collared pronghorn in the Madison (HD 360); HD 338 fell to 959 (31% below average) with 29.2 fawns per 100 does, the lowest since at least 1997.

Region 3 has lost about a third of its pronghorn over 15 years; HD 300's 2024 minimum count was about 49% of its long-term average. FWP capped Region 3 archery at 500 permits for 2026-27 and cut some rifle tags by up to half.
Region 7 fawn ratios dropped to 56 per 100 does in 2023 after drought, then rebounded to 73 in 2024.

bear.summary: Montana hasn't had a new black bear population estimate since a study that ended in 2011 put the number at about 13,000, so harvest is the main yardstick. Harvest climbed to a record 2,159 bears in 2022 and has settled around 1,500-1,650 since, with several island-range units taking more females than FWP's 40% guideline. A new statewide study began in 2023.

findings.text: FWP's only modeled statewide estimate is about 13,307 black bears, from a 2001-2011 DNA hair-snag and telemetry study; FWP still uses 'about 13,000' publicly.

FWP says there was no direct population monitoring between 2010 and 2023; a new multi-year study using hair corrals, about 800 trail cameras and GPS collars began in the Blackfoot in 2023 and BMU 103 in 2024.
Statewide harvest rose from about 1,200 bears a year (2007-2009) to a record 2,159 in 2022, then 1,484 (2023), 1,609 (2024) and 1,654 (2025); spring harvest topped 1,000 every year from 2020 on.
Females made up 31-39% of the statewide harvest every year, under FWP's 40% limit; the highest share was 39% in 2023.
In 2025, BMU 319 (Bridger Mountains) and BMU 316 ran 49% female and BMU 520 (Beartooths) 42%; a 2024 FWP analysis put BMU 520 at 25-30% below objective and still declining (secondary source).
Region 1 harvest fell from 749 in 2022 to 457 in 2023 and its share of the state's harvest dropped from about 46% (1987-2006) to about 29% (2023-2025).
Northwest Montana bears first reproduced successfully at age 6 or older, averaging 1.75 cubs every 3.2 years; a stable population needs adult survival of about 0.88.
In 2026, drought, early green-up and May frosts caused one of the worst natural bear food failures on record; Region 2 logged nearly 300 bear conflict reports in about two months.

events.text: About nine feet of snow near Glasgow from mid-November to April. Around 1,000 pronghorn were killed by trains, at least 200 died at one haystack, and 2,500-3,000 were stranded on Fort Peck Reservoir. FWP warned of major license cuts in HDs 630 and 670.
Nearly 400 dead whitetails west of Missoula and near Frenchtown in a confirmed EHD outbreak, the first documented west of the Continental Divide in Montana.
Two severe winters cut spring recruitment from 53 to 25 fawns per 100 adults. FWP removed either-sex days and made HD 130 buck-only starting in 2019.
After a summer drought, an epic winter cut Hi-Line mule deer 20-30% in spring surveys. Pronghorn were the biologist's top worry; elk wintered well.
Cold, deep snow and late green-up dropped HD 512 to 264 pronghorn in 2018 (lowest since 1981) with 23 fawns per 100 does. Either-sex licenses were cut from 75 to 50 in 2019.
Drought plus hard winters drove Region 7 mule deer to about 48-52% below the long-term average. Antlerless B licenses fell from 11,000 (2020) to 1,000 (2023-2025).

Drought-linked EHD outbreak along the Milk and Missouri rivers, the Yellowstone between Glendive and Sidney and much of Carter County, mostly in whitetails. FWP cut Region 6 surplus whitetail B licenses by 2,000.
After low spring counts, the Commission made 15 districts buck-only for mule deer: HD 301, HDs 410-471, HDs 621-622 and HDs 700-705.

Record early snow and cold. More than 30% of collared Madison pronghorn died, HD 338 had its lowest fawn ratio since at least 1997 (29.2 per 100 does), and early snow pushed elk onto winter range during rifle season. FWP eliminated B licenses in HDs 317, 338 and 339 and cut HD 310 quotas.
Bitter cold and long-lasting snowpack left spring 2023 whitetail recruitment highly variable, from 17 (HD 120) to 45 (HD 123) fawns per 100 adults; 2023 check-station harvest was flat at 761.

Missouri River Breaks elk fell to 56% below average and 41% below objective. For 2024 FWP cut Breaks antlerless elk licenses 69% and Region 6 mule deer B licenses from 6,200 to 2,825 (then to 1,425 in 2025).
Mild winters drove recovery: Region 7 pronghorn counts in 2025 were the highest since 2008, and by 2026 Region 6 mule deer were slightly above average with Region 7 at 17% below.

A localized EHD outbreak hit Glendive and Intake in 2024. In 2025 suspected EHD/bluetongue killed deer near Eureka, Plains and Missoula and in the northeast; the Commission capped Region 6 B licenses at 2,000, and spring 2026 recruitment in HDs 201/202 fell to 15-18 fawns per 100 adults.

With Region 3 pronghorn down about a third over 15 years, the Commission capped Region 3 archery at 500 permits for 2026-27, pulled the region from the 900-series archery tag and cut some rifle either-sex tags by up to half.

Drought, January-February green-up and May frosts caused one of the worst natural bear food failures on record (huckleberry, chokecherry, serviceberry). Region 2 logged nearly 300 bear conflict reports in about two months.
